The exact layout of every message and command is in the API reference.

docs.title: Over CAN
docs.text: CAN is the interface for running a machine: compact frames, a fixed cost per message, up to 14 drivers on one bus, and a host that can be a PC, a microcontroller or a robot control box. The driver answers a motion command with its position, speed and current in the same frame exchange, so a control loop on the host needs one frame out and one frame back per motor and cycle.

docs.title: The frame
docs.text:
CAN 2.0 data frames with 11-bit identifiers at 1 Mbit/s. The identifier carries the node, the command and the error state:

Figure 6.2: Bits 10 to 7 of the identifier are the node ID, bits 6 to 1 the command ID, bit 0 the error bit.
  • Node ID, bits 10 to 7: which driver, 0 to 15. A driver acts only on frames with its own node ID and sends with it. Set it with #CANID or Send_CAN_ID and save; every driver ships as node 0. Use 0 to 13: the bootloader reserves 14 and 15, and a driver on one of those cannot be updated over CAN.
  • Command ID, bits 6 to 1: which message, 0 to 63. The CAN reference lists all of them.
  • Error bit, bit 0: in a frame from the driver, 1 while any error is active. In a frame from the host it is ignored.

So a host sends Send_data_pack_1 (command 2) to node 3 with the identifier (3 << 7) | (2 << 1) = 0x184, and the driver answers with command 3 under (3 << 7) | (3 << 1) | error. A lower node ID wins the bus arbitration.

Multi-byte values are big-endian: the most significant byte is in data[0] and goes first. Floats are IEEE 754 single precision. Flags inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit.

docs.title: Three kinds of message
docs.text:
• Send_…: the host sends data. Some of these are answered (a motion command with Respond_data_pack_1, the gripper command with Respond_Gripper_data_pack); most are not.
  • Send_Respond_…: the host asks for data with a remote frame (the RTR bit set, no data) carrying the command ID; the driver answers with a data frame with the same command ID.
  • Respond_…: frames only the driver sends: the answers above, and the heartbeat.

docs.title: A control loop
docs.text:
Send Send_data_pack_1 at a fixed rate, 100 Hz to 1 kHz, with the setpoint for this cycle; read Respond_data_pack_1 for the position, speed and current of the last cycle. Every valid motion frame, and every status request the driver answers, resets the watchdog; the setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear, Save) do not. So with Send_Watchdog set to a few cycle times the motor stops when the host stops. A watchdog kept with Send_Save_config runs from power-up: a host that does not start its loop within the watchdog time finds the driver in watchdog error, and clears it with Send_Clear_Error. The heartbeat is the other way round: Send_Heartbeat_Setup makes the driver send a frame on its own every N ms when it has nothing else to send, so the host can see it is alive.

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant D as Driver
    H->>D: Send_Clear_Error
    H->>D: Send_Watchdog: a few cycle times
    H->>D: Send_Heartbeat_Setup: every N ms
    loop every cycle, 100 Hz to 1 kHz
        H->>D: Send_data_pack_1: the setpoint, with the feedforwards
        D-->>H: Respond_data_pack_1: position, speed, current, the error bit
    end
    D-->>H: heartbeat, whenever nothing else was sent for N ms
    Note over D: no motion frame or status request within the watchdog time: watchdog error, the motor stops

docs.title: From a PC
docs.text: The CANvas adapter shows up as a serial port and speaks slcan; python-can opens it with bustype='slcan'. The Python library wraps the whole protocol, see With Python. Any CAN adapter that python-can supports works the same way.

docs.title: Several drivers
docs.text: Give each driver its own node ID before you put them on one bus (a bus with two node 0s cannot tell them apart): connect one driver at a time over UART, #CANID 3, #Save. Terminate the first and the last node, and wire the daisy chain as in Power and the CAN daisy chain.

docs.title: Errors and recovery
docs.text: When the driver detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle, turns the status LED on steadily and sets the error bit in every CAN frame it sends. It stays there until the error is cleared.

docs.title: Seeing the error
docs.text:
• The LED: on and not flashing means error mode (or not calibrated). Three short flashes and a pause is normal operation; fast flashing is calibration.
  • #Error prints In error state! or No errors!, followed by one line per active error.
  • Send_Respond_State_of_Errors returns every flag as a bit; the error bit of any frame says whether there is one.
Normal operation Calibration Error mode

In error mode the LED does not flash: it stays on, as in the photo on the right.

docs.title: The errors
docs.text: Error #Error line Cause What to do Vbus Vbus error the supply voltage is below 9 V or above 29 V (#Vmax, 29000 mV after #Default) check the supply and the cable; a decelerating motor can push the voltage up Encoder Encoder error the encoder reports no magnet: missing, too far away or too weak magnet distance and type, see The encoder magnet Driver Driver error (undervoltage, thermal shutdown, or overcurrent) reserved: this firmware never raises it, because it does not monitor the driver stage — Velocity Velocity error the speed passed 30,000,000 ticks/s, a fixed threshold that #Vlimit does not change; in practice only a runaway reaches it check the magnet and the calibration Temperature Temp error the thermistor reads more than #Tlim (75 °C by default), with #Term 1 let the motor cool; lower the current limit E-stop Received ESTOP command Send_ESTOP was received clear it when it is safe Watchdog Watchdog error no motion frame or status request within the watchdog time (Send_Watchdog) the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear Not calibrated Not calibrated the motor has not been calibrated since #Default, or the EEPROM is invalid run #Cal and #Save Current Current error reserved; this firmware never raises it —

docs.title: Clearing
docs.text: #Clear or Send_Clear_Error clears the flags and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back: a Vbus error at 2 V stays until the supply is right; once the supply is 24 V, one #Clear returns the driver to normal operation. The calibration error clears only by calibrating (or, for a motor you know is calibrated, #Calibrated 1). A gripper E-stop comes back on every control cycle until its E-stop bit is 0 again: #Gripstop 0, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit clear; then clear. While it is active, #Error prints only In error state!.

docs.title: When the driver does not answer
docs.text:
• No LED at all: no power. Check DC+ and DC− and the cable orientation.
  • LED on, no answer on UART: the baud rate (256000), TX and RX crossed, the adapter's port.
  • No answer on CAN: the node ID, the termination (about 60 Ω across the bus, unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter.
  • #Info shows -1 or nonsense: with firmware 106 and newer this should not happen, because the driver replaces a damaged configuration block with the defaults at power-up. If it does, #Default, then calibrate again.

Troubleshooting goes through the symptoms one by one.

docs.title: Gripper mode
docs.text: A driver can run a gripper instead of a joint: the same board, with a state machine that moves a jaw to a position between open and closed, at a speed, with a current limit that becomes the grip force, and that reports when it holds something. The MSG gripper is built on STEPFOC this way.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
#Gripper 1
#Save

#Default clears the flag again. A driver in gripper mode still answers every other command; the gripper commands only work with the flag set.

docs.title: Calibrating the gripper
docs.text:
After every power-up the gripper has to find its end stops: #Gripcal or Send_gripper_calibrate. The jaws open until they stop, then close until they stop, slowly and at 500 mA; the positions become 0 (open) and 255 (closed). The driver prints nothing when it is done. If it has not found both end stops within about 24 s it gives up, and the gripper stays uncalibrated. Check the result with #Gripinfo (Gripper calibrated is: 1) or the gripper_calibrated bit of Respond_Gripper_data_pack: a move is carried out only once the gripper is calibrated. The motor itself must be calibrated (#Cal) and saved before that, once.

While the gripper calibrates, send only empty status polls. A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or #Clear stops the calibration without a message, and the next one then starts part way through, where the stopped one left off: switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again (known issue KI-7).

docs.title: Moving
docs.text:
Over UART:

#Gripvel 100       speed, 0 to 255
#Gripcur 400       current limit of the move in mA, the grip force
#Grippos 200       go to position 200 (0 open, 255 closed); also activates the gripper

Over CAN, Send_gripper_data_pack carries position, speed and current in one frame with the activate and action bits; the driver answers with Respond_Gripper_data_pack: the position, the measured current, whether it is moving, and the object detection:

Object detection Meaning 0 moving 1 an object was detected while closing: the jaws stopped on it and hold it with the current limit 2 an object was detected while opening 3 the position was reached

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack (0 bytes) only asks for the state. The answer to a 5-byte command goes out before the driver acts on it, so its object detection and error bits are still those of the moment before (KI-6); the answers to the next frames show the new move. The action bit in the answer is a copy of the last command's action bit and stays 1 after the move ends (KI-8): the object detection tells when it has ended.

Send_gripper_data_pack's E-stop bit raises the gripper E-stop error; #Gripstop 1 does the same over UART. The error stays: while the E-stop bit is 1 the driver raises it again on every control cycle, and #Error prints only In error state!. To recover, clear the bit (#Gripstop 0, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit 0), then #Clear or Send_Clear_Error.

Current

The firmware does not limit the current you give a gripper move. The safe range depends on the gripper's mechanics and motor; the gripper's manual gives it. The driver is rated for 2.8 A, but nothing enforces that here: a gripper move uses the current as sent.

docs.title: Where the details are
docs.text: The bytes of the two gripper frames are in the CAN reference, the UART commands in the UART reference.

docs.title: Control modes
docs.text:
The driver is always in one control mode. A command that carries a setpoint switches to the mode that uses it; #Idle or Send_Idle switches back to idle. The driver refuses every mode except idle, open loop included, while it is not calibrated or while an error is active.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotCalibrated: power-up, no saved calibration
    [*] --> Idle: power-up, saved calibration
    NotCalibrated --> Calibration: #Cal
    Calibration --> Idle: success, #Save
    Calibration --> NotCalibrated: a test fails
    Idle --> ControlMode: a setpoint
    ControlMode --> Idle: #Idle, Send_Idle
    ControlMode --> Error: a fault
    Idle --> Error: a fault
    Error --> Idle: #Clear, cause gone

A setpoint is #P, #V, #Iq, #PD or a CAN motion frame, and a new setpoint switches the mode without passing through idle; a fault is any of the errors on Errors and recovery.

ControlMode What the motor does Entered by Setpoint unit Idle nothing: brakes (phases shorted), the default, or coasts (phases open), as set by #Brake / #Coast or Send_Settings; see Braking in idle #Idle, Send_Idle, #Clear, errors — Position holds and moves to a position with the cascade of position, velocity and current loops #P, Send_data_pack_1 (8 bytes) encoder ticks Velocity turns at a speed with the velocity and current loops #V, Send_data_pack_1 (5 bytes) encoder ticks/s Current (torque) applies a current, so a torque, with the current loop alone #Iq, Send_data_pack_1 (2 bytes) mA PD (impedance) behaves like a spring and a damper around a position, with KP and KD #PD, Send_data_pack_PD encoder ticks Voltage torque applies a voltage on the q axis directly, without the current loop: clamped to #Vlim, not current-limited #Uq mV Open loop steps the motor like a plain stepper driver, without the encoder and without a current limit; see Open-loop stepping #Openloop (continuous), #gosteps (a number of microsteps) electrical rad/s; microsteps HALL spins until a sensor on ADDITIONAL2 triggers, then holds the position reached; with a level trigger only while the pin stays at that level #HALL, Send_data_pack_HALL encoder ticks/s Gripper runs the gripper state machine: move to a jaw position with a speed and a current limit #Grippos, Send_gripper_data_pack (with #Gripper 1) 0 to 255 Calibration the calibration routine, and the angle-offset step alone #Cal, #Calangle, #Gripcal —

docs.title: Braking in idle
docs.text:
In idle the driver brakes: it keeps both coils shorted through the driver stage, so the motor resists being turned. It does so at every power-up, and also with an error, which puts the driver in idle. #Coast (or Send_Settings over CAN) lets the motor coast instead, with the coils open, until the next power-up: #Save does not keep it. #Brake brakes again.

The braking current is not limited

A motor that is turned while it brakes drives its own back-EMF current through the shorted coils, and the current loop does not limit that current. Do not let a load drive a braking motor fast; send #Coast first when the shaft must turn freely.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• Position is in encoder ticks: 16384 per revolution of the motor shaft, counting up without limit over several revolutions. Positive is counter-clockwise seen from the magnet (the back of the motor).
  • Speed is in encoder ticks per second: 16384 is one revolution per second, 60 rpm.
  • Current is in mA. Torque is current times the motor's Kt, which calibration finds.
  • Feedforward: the 8-byte motion frame carries a speed and a current feedforward beside the position, the 5-byte one a current feedforward beside the speed. They are added after the loops, so a host that knows the trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct the rest. Send 0 when you do not use them.

docs.text:

As a position: 1.000 turns, 360.0° · as a speed: 60 rpm · the practical maximum for 50 pole pairs is about 720 rpm

The units of this page, with your numbers: 16384 encoder ticks per turn, the practical speed limit from the electrical frequency the control loop can follow (Ratings and limits), and the torque as Kt times the current.

docs.title: Open-loop stepping
docs.text:
#Openloop and #gosteps drive the coils like a plain stepper driver, without the encoder in the loop. Like every other mode, they need a calibrated driver without errors.

  • #Openloop 50 turns the field at 50 electrical rad/s and keeps turning until another command. On a motor with 50 pole pairs that is 50 ÷ (2π × 50), about 0.16 revolutions per second.
  • #gosteps 64 makes 64 microsteps, then goes to idle; a negative number goes the other way. #microstep (16 by default) is the number of microsteps per electrical cycle, which is four full steps: with 16, #gosteps 16 turns a 1.8° motor by 7.2°. #stepinterval (1000 µs by default) is the time between two microsteps, rounded down to whole control cycles of 160 µs.
  • #Openv (5000 mV by default) is the voltage both put on the coils.

None of these settings is saved.

Open loop is not current-limited

Open loop applies a voltage, not a current, and #Ilim does not apply. At standstill and low speed the coil current is about #Openv ÷ R: the default 5000 mV drives about 4.5 A through a 1.1 Ω coil, more than the driver's 2.8 A and the motor's rating. Set #Openv to the rated current × R first (2 A × 1.1 Ω = 2200 mV), and keep the test short.

docs.title: Positive rotation
docs.text: Figure 6.1: Positive rotation is counter-clockwise looking at the encoder magnet. A positive current turns the motor that way, a positive speed too, and the position grows.

docs.title: Which mode am I in?
docs.text: #Mode prints the mode: Idle mode, Position control, Speed control, Current control, PD control, Open loop, Gripper mode or Gripper calib mode. In this firmware release the voltage-torque mode reads Gripper mode too (a leftover label), and HALL mode, the angle-offset search (#Calangle), open-loop steps (#gosteps) and gripper mode print nothing. The behaviour of the motor is the reliable check there.

docs.title: Working in Motor GUI
docs.text: Everyday use of the driver from Motor GUI: moving the motor, watching it, recording what it does, running several motors, and the few things that only work from the console.

docs.title: Moving the motor
docs.text: The jog controls send setpoints in the matching control mode: Jog velocity turns the motor at a speed in encoder ticks per second (16384 is one revolution per second), Jog position moves it to a position in ticks, Jog current applies a torque in mA. Send setpoint sends a value in the mode the driver is in. Idle stops the motor; Control modes says what each mode does. With Live stream while dragging the setpoint follows the slider, which is the quickest way to feel a tuning change.

docs.title: Watching it
docs.text: The plots show position, speed and current as the driver reports them. Pan and zoom to a move; hover for the value. A step in the position setpoint shows overshoot and settling at once, a speed step shows the velocity loop's response; Current limit and loop tuning uses them step by step.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text: A recording keeps the telemetry stream to a file: New recording, run the move, Stop recording. Record the response before and after a tuning change to compare them, or a failure to attach to a bug report (Report a problem).

docs.title: Clearing errors
docs.text: The errors the driver reports are listed with the state; Clear errors sends what #Clear does. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; Errors and recovery says what each one needs.

docs.title: Several motors
docs.text: Over the CANvas adapter the GUI sees every driver on the bus and addresses each by its node ID. Give each driver its own ID over the serial adapter first (the CAN node ID in the settings, then Save), terminate the first and the last node, and set a watchdog (Watchdog ms) on a bus that drives something that must not run away: Power and the CAN daisy chain, Over CAN.

docs.title: Gripper
docs.text: A driver in gripper mode shows the gripper controls: calibrate the jaws, a position from open to closed, a speed, a current limit, and the state the gripper reports. No gripper connection means the driver is not in gripper mode or not on the bus. Gripper mode.

docs.title: Firmware updates
docs.text: Firmware update lists the releases from GitHub and flashes one through the bootloader; on a bus, Scan bootloaders finds the boards. Updating through the bootloader.

docs.title: The console
docs.text: Anything the GUI has no control for is one # command away in the console, with the driver's answer below it; the whole set is in the UART commands reference. The cyclic output (#Cyc) is what the GUI's telemetry stream uses over serial, so do not start it by hand while the plots run.

docs.title: With Python
docs.text: The Spectral-BLDC library wraps the CAN protocol: one method per message, and the driver's answers unpacked into attributes. It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS with any adapter python-can supports, such as the CANvas adapter over slcan.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
In a virtual environment:

WindowsLinuxmacOS 

py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install Spectral-BLDC
The CANvas adapter is COM and a number (Device Manager, Ports (COM & LPT)): channel='COM41'.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install Spectral-BLDC
sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER     # access to the serial port; log out and in again once
The CANvas adapter is /dev/ttyACM0 (ls /dev/ttyACM* lists it): channel='/dev/ttyACM0'.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install Spectral-BLDC
The CANvas adapter is /dev/cu.usbmodem and a number (ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* lists it): channel='/dev/cu.usbmodem1101', with your number.

Check

python -c "import Spectral_BLDC" returns without an error message.

The source and the examples are in Spectral-BLDC-Python. For joints with a gear ratio and an offset, the Source Robotics Toolbox (pip install SourceRoboticsToolbox) turns encoder ticks into joint angles.

docs.title: The first program
docs.text:
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# the adapter: a CANvas on COM41 (Windows) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux), 1 Mbit/s
comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# the driver with node ID 0
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

motor.Send_Clear_Error()

# A configured, calibrated motor with a clear shaft: command one turn for five seconds.
# Each command requests a fresh position/speed/current reply; heartbeat is not required.
try:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 5.0
    next_cycle = time.monotonic()
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        motor.Send_data_pack_1(Position=16384, Speed=0, Current=0)
        reply_deadline = min(deadline, time.monotonic() + 0.02)
        while time.monotonic() < reply_deadline:
            message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(
                timeout=max(0.0, reply_deadline - time.monotonic()))
            if message is None:
                print("No motion feedback in this cycle; check the bus and node ID")
                break
            if ids.node_id != 0 or ids.command_id != 3:  # Respond_data_pack_1
                continue
            motor.UnpackData(message, ids)
            print(motor.position, motor.speed, motor.current, ids.error_bit)
            if ids.error_bit:
                raise RuntimeError("Driver fault: inspect State_of_Errors before retrying")
            break
        next_cycle += 0.02
        time.sleep(max(0.0, next_cycle - time.monotonic()))
finally:
    motor.Send_Idle()                    # also on Ctrl-C; the shaft no longer holds torque

receive_can_messages returns the raw python-can message and a tuple with the node ID, the command ID and the error bit of the identifier; UnpackData decodes the message into the attributes the message carries. This example resends the same setpoint at 50 Hz for five seconds, prints only matching motion feedback, and puts the motor in idle when it ends. Idle releases torque: support any attached mechanism before running it. A missing reply is reported without claiming that a move finished. Configure and calibrate the driver first (Quick start).

Check

The program prints a line of position, speed, current and error bit for each cycle, the position moves to 16384 and the error bit stays 0. No motion feedback in this cycle means no answer came back: the port, the node ID and the bus, see Over CAN.

docs.title: What is where
docs.text:
Library call Message What you get back Send_data_pack_1(Position, Speed, Current) Send_data_pack_1 position, speed, current Send_data_pack_PD(...) Send_data_pack_PD position, speed, current Send_Respond_Encoder_data() Send_Respond_Encoder_data position, speed (32-bit) Send_Respond_State_of_Errors() Send_Respond_State_of_Errors the error attributes Send_gripper_data_pack(...) Send_gripper_data_pack gripper_position, gripper_current, the gripper state bits Send_Limits(...), Send_Velocity_Gains(...), ... the setting messages nothing; Send_Save_config() keeps them

The complete map of calls to messages is in the Python library reference, and each message's bytes in the CAN reference.

docs.title: Several motors
docs.text:
One CanCommunication per bus, one SpectralCAN per driver with its node ID. Send to each, then read the bus: every answer carries the node ID in ids.node_id, so route it to the right object.

motors = [Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=i, communication=comms) for i in range(3)]
for m in motors:
    m.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
for _ in motors:
    message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.1)
    if message is not None:
        motors[ids.node_id].UnpackData(message, ids)

The Guides build on this: a quadruped leg, gravity compensation, bilateral teleoperation.

docs.title: Over UART
docs.text: The serial port is the interactive way to use the driver: you type a command, the driver answers in text. It is the only way to calibrate, and the quickest way to try a setting. For real-time control of several motors use CAN.

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
A command is #, a name, optionally a space and one number, and a line ending:

#P 16384
#P
#Cal
  • The name is case-sensitive and matches the firmware's spelling exactly (#Kpiq, not #kpiq); at most 19 characters, the number at most 19 characters, both together at most 20.
  • The line ends with LF (\n); a CR before it is accepted. Terminals send CR+LF when you press Enter, with the setting described in The serial terminal.
  • A Set/Get command with a number sets the value and prints it; without a number it only prints it. #P 16384 moves to position 16384 and prints the position; #P prints the position.
  • An action command takes no number: #Cal, #Save, #Idle.
  • A command the parser does not know is answered with Unknown command (firmware 106 and newer). A few names the parser accepts have no handler and are answered with nothing; the UART reference lists them.
  • 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V.

docs.title: The driver only answers
docs.text: The driver never sends anything on its own, except with the cyclic commands: #Cyc 100 makes it print position, speed and Iq every 100 ms as $ <position> <speed> <Iq> (for BetterSerialPlotter), #Cyca 100 as Position:x,Speed:y,Iq:z (for the Arduino plotter); #Cyc or #Cyca without a number stops it.

docs.title: Typical sessions
docs.text:
A first test after calibration:

#Ilim 1500        current limit for the motor
#V 16384          one revolution per second
#V 0
#P 0              back to the start
#Idle

Tuning:

#Kpv 0.02
#Kiv 0.001
#V 30000
#Save

Status:

#Info
#Error
#Temp
#Vbus

Every command is in the UART reference, grouped by what it does.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text: The driver's firmware is open source and released as numbered builds. A driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a bootloader and updates itself over UART or CAN, and so do some drivers shipped before 105, which report 103 (Drivers that report 103 says how to tell). A driver without the bootloader needs it installed once with a programming adapter.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Releases and versions: how releases are numbered, how to see which one a driver runs, what the release notes contain
  • The bootloader: what it is, how the driver boots, how it is entered, its protocol and tools
  • Updating through the bootloader: the normal update, with Motor GUI, the bootloader's command-line tool, or a PAR6 control box
  • Installing the bootloader on an older board: for a driver that runs firmware 103 or older
  • Building from source: PlatformIO, the memory layout, uploading with a programming adapter

The release notes of every release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix, Firmware release notes.

docs.title: Installing the bootloader on an older board
docs.text:
A driver running release 103 or older from the main branch has no bootloader: its firmware starts at the beginning of the flash. A driver that reports 103 may have the bootloader all the same; check first, as in Drivers that report 103. To run any release from 105 on, which is linked to start above the bootloader, the bootloader must be installed once, with a programming adapter on the JTAG connector. After that, every update goes over UART or CAN.

Warning

Disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter before connecting the programming adapter. The adapter powers the board at 3.3 V.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The programming adapter (an ST-LINK with the 1.27 mm pogo-pin adapter for the JTAG pads), or any ST-LINK, J-Link or OpenOCD-compatible probe wired to 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO and SWCLK.
  • STM32CubeProgrammer or the older STM32 ST-LINK Utility on the PC, with the ST-LINK drivers.
  • The bootloader binary from the bootloader repository's bin/ folder; its README.md names the current file.
WindowsLinuxmacOS

STM32CubeProgrammer or the ST-LINK Utility, and the ST-LINK USB driver (STSW-LINK009) for the adapter.

STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver, but your user needs access to its USB device: install the udev rules that come with STM32CubeProgrammer, or run it with sudo.

STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver.

Figure 7.1: The JTAG pads, marked 3V3, GND, SWCLK, SWDIO. The adapter is pressed onto them; a little pressure makes the contact.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Connect the adapter to the JTAG pads and the PC.
  2. In the programmer, connect to the target (SWD). The STM32F103CB shows up with 128 KB of flash.
  3. Erase the chip, or at least the application region: the old firmware and the bootloader must not overlap.
  4. Program the bootloader binary at address 0x08000000.
  5. Disconnect the adapter, power the driver. The bootloader finds no valid application and waits in bootloader mode, with the LED blinking.
  6. Flash the firmware release through the bootloader, over UART or CAN, as in Updating through the bootloader.
  7. #Info shows the new release. #Default, enter the motor parameters, calibrate, #Save.

Check

#Info prints the release you flashed, and a driver powered up while bl_flash.py list or Motor GUI's Scan bootloaders is polling answers in its first two seconds: the bootloader is there. If the firmware does not start, see Updating through the bootloader: when it fails.

Memory layout

0x08000000–0x080022FF bootloader, 0x08002C00 its configuration page (board ID, the application's CRC), 0x08003000–0x0801FFFF the application (116 KB). The bootloader keeps a magic value in RAM to hand over to the application in about 10 ms on a normal boot.

docs.title: The programmer's settings
docs.text:
In ST-LINK Utility, Target → Settings with SWD and the default frequency works; Target → Program & Verify with the start address 0x08000000. The pictures of the old flashing procedure apply to the connection and the settings dialog:

Settings Programming

The same adapter uploads a firmware you build yourself, see Building from source.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text: The firmware is a PlatformIO project for the Arduino core on the STM32F103CB, in the STEPFOC firmware folder of the firmware repository on the bootloader-version branch.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
1. Install Visual Studio Code and the PlatformIO extension.
  2. Clone the repository and check out bootloader-version.
  3. Open the STEPFOC firmware folder in VS Code; PlatformIO fetches the platform (ststm32@15.4.1) and builds with the PlatformIO Build button or pio run. The image is .pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin.

The project is linked for the bootloader: VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000, the linker script ldscript_bootloader.ld, the upload offset 0x08003000 and a maximum size of 118784 bytes, in platformio.ini. A build that exceeds the size fails to link.

Check

PlatformIO ends the build with SUCCESS, and .pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin is there. If it fails, the first error above the summary names the cause.

docs.title: Uploading
docs.text:
PlatformIO runs on Windows, Linux and macOS alike. On Linux, an upload with the programming adapter also needs PlatformIO's udev rules (99-platformio-udev.rules, in the PlatformIO documentation), and a serial port the dialout group.

  • Through the bootloader: flash the built firmware.bin with bl_flash.py or Motor GUI as in Updating through the bootloader. This is how a release is installed, and works on any driver with the bootloader.
  • With the programming adapter: Upload in PlatformIO uses ST-LINK and writes the image at 0x08003000. It leaves the bootloader alone, but it does not update the image CRC the bootloader keeps; see the warning below. The serial monitor (the plug icon) opens the UART at 256000 with send_on_enter, so you can type commands to the driver from the same window.

After an ST-LINK upload the firmware does not start

At every power-up the bootloader checks the firmware against the CRC it stored at the last flash through the bootloader. After an upload with the programming adapter that CRC no longer matches, so the bootloader stays in bootloader mode, with the LED blinking, instead of starting the new firmware. Flash the same firmware.bin once more through the bootloader to recover. Once the bootloader is on the board, install every firmware through it.

Figure 7.2: Build, upload and the serial monitor in PlatformIO's status bar.

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text: release_guide.md in the repository is the procedure: bump FIRMWARE_VERSION, build, commit the source change with the rebuilt Binaries/firmware.bin, tag V<number>, create the GitHub release with the image and firmware.json and the release notes. This site's tools/sync_firmware.py reads a release by its tag; the version box names the release.

docs.title: A firmware for a board without a bootloader
docs.text: The main branch builds a firmware linked at 0x08000000 for boards that have no bootloader. It stops at release 103 and is not maintained; install the bootloader instead, Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: Releases and versions
docs.text: A firmware release is a number: 103, 105, 106, … Every release is a tag V<number> in the firmware repository and a GitHub release that carries the image stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin, a manifest firmware.json with the image's size, SHA-256 and the commit it was built from, and the release notes. The notes are the firmware's changelog; the appendix collects them.

docs.title: Which release does my driver run?
docs.text:
#Info

prints Software version: <number> among the rest; Motor GUI shows the same number in the driver's identity, and over CAN Send_Respond_Device_Info returns it as the third byte. From firmware 105 the number is the build's own version. Before that it was read from the EEPROM, where the last #Default wrote it, so it names the firmware that last restored the defaults, not necessarily the one running: 101 and 102 write 101, 103 writes 103.

docs.title: Drivers that report 103
docs.text:
A driver that reports 103 runs either release 103 from the main branch, without a bootloader, or an early build of the bootloader-version branch, which also writes 103 and runs above the bootloader. Some drivers were shipped with the bootloader before release 105. Which image those carry was not recorded: most likely 103, built for the bootloader.

To tell whether yours has the bootloader:

  • Watch the LED as you switch the driver on: with the bootloader it blinks for about two seconds before the firmware starts.
  • Or power it up while bl_flash.py list or Motor GUI's Scan bootloaders is polling: a driver with the bootloader answers in its first two seconds.

With the bootloader, update it to the current release as in Updating through the bootloader; the release it ran before does not matter then. Without one, install it first: Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: Which release does this site describe?
docs.text: The one in the version box on the landing page and in the version selector in the header. When a newer release changes what a page says, a new version of the site is published and the previous one stays reachable from the selector. The compatibility table says which releases go with which bootloader, Python library and PAR6 runtime.

docs.title: The Spectral Micro counterpart
docs.text: A change that applies to both drivers comes to the Spectral Micro too, but not always in a release with the same number: STEPFOC 108 matches Spectral Micro 107. The compatibility table lists the pairs.

docs.title: The two branches
docs.text: Releases from 105 on are built from the bootloader-version branch of the repository, whose firmware is linked to run above the bootloader. The main branch holds the firmware of release 103 and earlier, linked to run without a bootloader, and is not updated. A board running 103 is documented by version 103 of this site; to move it to a current release, see Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: The bootloader
docs.text: Every driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a small bootloader in the first 12 KB of its flash. It starts the firmware on a normal boot, and it loads a new firmware over UART or CAN when a host asks, so a driver is updated without a programming adapter and without opening anything. The bootloader is open source: stm32f103c-bootloader, shared with the Spectral Micro.

docs.title: Memory layout
docs.text:
Address Contents 0x08000000 – 0x080022FF the bootloader (about 9 KB) 0x08002C00 – 0x08002FFF the bootloader's configuration page: the board ID, the firmware's page count and CRC, the bootloader's build version 0x08003000 – 0x0801FFFF the firmware (up to 116 KB) RAM 0x20001000 a magic word the bootloader sets to hand over to the firmware

The firmware is linked to start at 0x08003000 and sets its vector table there (VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000); the first 0x3000 bytes belong to the bootloader and the firmware never touches them.

docs.title: What happens at boot
docs.text:
1. On a reset, the bootloader runs first. If the magic word is in RAM and the reset was a software reset, it checks the firmware's stack pointer and reset vector and jumps straight into the firmware: about 10 ms, the normal boot.
  2. Otherwise it initialises the clocks, CAN, UART and its watchdog, and listens for a host for 2 s. The LED flashes three times at the start, then blinks while the bootloader listens, faster while a host talks to it.
  3. With no host, and a firmware whose stored CRC is valid, it sets the magic word and resets; the next boot takes the fast path.
  4. With a host talking, it stays as long as the host keeps talking: 3 s after the last command, 60 s once a flash is in progress. Any PING resets the timer.
  5. With no valid firmware (never flashed, or a flash that was interrupted), it stays in bootloader mode and waits, with the LED blinking; the driver answers nothing on #Info.

docs.title: Entering the bootloader
docs.text:
• From the firmware: #Reset over UART or Send_Reset (command 14) over CAN. Since firmware 105 both reset the driver into the bootloader's 2 s window; the host tools send them for you.
  • At power-on: the 2 s window after every power-up, if the host is already polling.
  • Always, when there is no valid firmware.

docs.title: The board ID
docs.text: The bootloader has a board ID of its own, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. 14 and 15 do not exist for it: its command frame, identifier 0x700, decodes as node 14 in the firmware's identifier scheme, so those two node IDs are reserved. Give drivers node IDs 0 to 13. The firmware accepts #CANID 14 and 15, but the bootloader then keeps its old board ID and a firmware update over CAN cannot reach the driver. The firmware keeps the board ID in step with its CAN node ID when the configuration is saved: #Save or Send_Save_config writes the node ID into the bootloader's board ID, so a driver answers the host tools under its node ID. A node ID that is set but not saved is not the board ID yet. A replacement board ships as ID 0; two boards with the same ID on one bus corrupt each other's flash stream, so give the new board its ID alone on the bus first (set-id in the host tool).

docs.title: Transports and protocol
docs.text:
Over CAN (1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers) the host commands on identifier 0x700 with 8 data bytes (board_id, cmd, two parameters); the board replies on 0x701 + board_id with 5 bytes (board_id, cmd, error code, a 16-bit parameter); the firmware image streams in bulk frames on (board_id << 7) | sequence, 16 frames of 8 bytes per chunk, with no reply per frame. Over UART (256000 baud) the same commands travel in framed packets [0xBB][CMD][LEN][BOARD_ID][DATA…][CRC16] with the same 5-byte reply, but the first four have other numbers.

Commands over CAN: WBUF (1), WPAGE (2), WCRC (3), PING (4), SET_ID (5), ERASE_APP (6), STREAM_BEGIN (7), STREAM_STATUS (8). Over UART: PING (1), WBUF (2), WPAGE (3), WCRC (4), and the others as over CAN, plus STREAM_DATA (9), which carries the stream frames. Error codes: 0 OK, 1 invalid offset, 2 invalid CRC, 3 flash write failed, 4 invalid page number. A flash is: ping, reset the firmware if it answers, ping until the bootloader answers, ERASE_APP (about 3.5 s), then for each 1 KB page STREAM_BEGIN, 8 chunks of 16 frames, STREAM_STATUS, WPAGE with the page's CRC32; finally WCRC with the page count and the image's CRC32. The bootloader stores the CRC and reboots into the new firmware. The full wire protocol is in the bootloader repository's docs/PROTOCOL.md.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: An interrupted flash leaves an invalid CRC; the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits, so the board is not lost: flash again. A board that answers nothing at all: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the 2 s window. The one thing the tools refuse, and that would need a programming adapter to undo, is flashing an image linked for 0x08000000 (a firmware from the main branch) over the firmware region.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text: Boards that run release 103 or older from the main branch have no bootloader; some boards shipped before 105 have it although they report 103 (Drivers that report 103). Installing the bootloader on an older board puts it there once, with a programming adapter at 0x08000000; from then on the board updates like any other.

docs.title: Updating through the bootloader
docs.text:
A driver with the bootloader (firmware 105 or newer) is updated over the UART connector or the CAN bus: the host tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it. No programming adapter, and nothing to open.

Before you update

  • Park the mechanism: the motor loses torque during the update and until the new firmware is calibrated and commanded.
  • An update may clear the calibration (the release notes say so when it does); plan to calibrate and #Save afterwards, and note the gains #Info prints.
  • On a bus with several drivers, update each node; a bus with mixed releases behaves unpredictably.

docs.title: With Motor GUI
docs.text: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, connected over the serial adapter or the CANvas adapter: choose the release, and the GUI fetches the image and its manifest from the GitHub release, verifies the size and the SHA-256, resets the driver into its bootloader and flashes it. This is the way for one driver on the bench.

docs.title: With the bootloader's command-line tool
docs.text:
The bootloader repository has host_tools/bl_flash.py, which flashes an image over CAN (slcan or candleLight/gs_usb adapters) or over UART:

pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter on COM6, driver with board ID 0
python bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel COM6 flash stepfoc-firmware-V108.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART on COM7
python bl_flash.py --transport uart --port COM7 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V108.bin --board 0 --erase-first

cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0; ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* gives the name

The tool sends the reset command to the running firmware (#Reset over UART, Send_Reset over CAN), catches the bootloader's two-second window, erases the application pages and streams the image page by page, each page verified by a CRC; list shows the boards in bootloader mode, set-id changes a board's bootloader ID. The image is the stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin from the GitHub release.

Board ID and node ID

The bootloader has its own board ID (0 to 13), kept in its configuration page, separate from the firmware's CAN node ID. The firmware keeps the two in step when the configuration is saved (#Save, Send_Save_config), so a driver's bootloader ID is normally its node ID. After #CANID, save before you flash over CAN.

Check

After the flash, from Motor GUI or the tool, the driver starts the new firmware: #Info prints the release you flashed as Software version, and Motor GUI shows it in the driver's identity. If the driver does not answer, see When it fails.

docs.title: From a PAR6 control box
docs.text: A robot built on the Robot Control Box updates every joint from the box itself, over its own CAN bus, from the dashboard's Firmware tab or with tools/flash_motor_firmware.py; the PAR6 documentation describes it.

docs.title: What happens in the driver
docs.text:
1. The host sends the reset; the firmware reboots into the bootloader.
  2. The bootloader listens for two seconds. With no host it starts the firmware; with a host it stays as long as the host keeps talking (60 s during a flash).
  3. The application pages are erased, then written page by page; each page is checked by a CRC.
  4. The bootloader checks the whole image's CRC, records it, and starts the new firmware.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
A flash that fails or is cancelled part way is not a brick: the stored CRC is invalid, so the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits for a host. Run the flash again; bl_flash.py list (or a passive scan from the control box) finds the board. A board that answers nothing: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the two-second window.

An image linked for 0x08000000 (a firmware from the main branch, release 103 and earlier) must never be flashed through the bootloader: it would overwrite the bootloader's own region if the tool did not refuse it. The tools validate the image first.

docs.title: Low-quality motors
docs.text: Motors with visibly bad windings, an uneven back-EMF or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate poorly and run rough. The tested motors are known good.

docs.title: The magnet and the encoder
docs.text:
• The distance is 1 mm. "Magnet Good" from the magnet test does not mean the distance is right, only that the field is strong enough.
  • A magnet touching the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet too far gives a noisy, wrong position.
  • The magnet must be diametrically magnetised and centred on the shaft.

docs.title: The driver gets hot or shuts down
docs.text: The firmware does not monitor the driver stage: if the stage stops on its own, for heat or a short, the motor loses torque and no error is reported. Lower the current limit, give the board airflow, check the motor leads for a short. Near 2.8 A the driver needs cooling.

docs.title: STEPFOC firmware
docs.text:
Seen in: 108.

What happens What to do More KI-1 The current limit of Send_Limits over CAN is used as sent, also above the driver's 2800 mA; only #Ilim over UART clamps it. Keep the current limit your host sends within the motor's rating and 2800 mA. Send_Limits KI-2 Calibration sets the current limit to 1600 mA and leaves it there, whatever it was before; a #Save right after calibration stores the 1600 mA. After every calibration set #Ilim for your motor, then #Save. Calibration: save KI-3 The serial number is not read back from the EEPROM at power-up, so #SERNUM, Motor GUI and Send_Respond_Device_Info report 1, and every #Save writes that 1 over the stored number. Tell drivers apart by their CAN node ID. To keep a serial number stored, set it with #SERNUM before every #Save. Saving the configuration KI-4 For anyone reading or changing the source, the start values in common.h are not the factory defaults (the gripper and calibrated flags start at 1, the pole pairs at 50, Max_Vbus at 29500 mV). The EEPROM replaces them at power-up, so a running driver does not show them. Take the defaults from the Defaults page, which lists what #Default writes, or from Set_Default_config() in EEPROM.cpp. Defaults KI-5 While the E-stop bit of the last Send_gripper_data_pack (or #Gripstop 1) is 1, the driver raises the gripper E-stop error again on every control cycle, so Send_Clear_Error or #Clear alone does not clear it. Send a gripper frame with the E-stop bit 0 (or #Gripstop 0) first, then clear the error. Gripper mode: moving KI-6 The answer to a 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack goes out before the driver has acted on the command, so its object detection and error bits are those of the moment before, for example 3 (position reached) from the previous move. Judge the new move by the answers to later frames, or poll with an empty Send_gripper_data_pack. Gripper mode: moving KI-7 A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or #Clear during the gripper calibration stops it without a message and leaves its counters as they were, so the next calibration starts part way through; it may skip the opening or give up early. Send only empty status polls while the gripper calibrates (up to about 24 s). After an interrupted calibration, switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again. Gripper mode: calibrating KI-8 The action bit in Respond_Gripper_data_pack is a copy of the last command's action bit; the driver never clears it, so it stays 1 after the move has ended. Tell the end of a move by the object detection, 3 position reached, 1 or 2 stopped on an object. Respond_Gripper_data_pack KI-9 Open loop (#Openloop, #gosteps) puts #Openv on the coils without a current limit; #Ilim does not apply. The default 5000 mV drives about 4.5 A through a 1.1 Ω coil. Set #Openv to the motor's rated current times its phase resistance first, and keep open-loop tests short. Open-loop stepping KI-10 The velocity error trips only above a fixed 30,000,000 ticks/s, about 1830 revolutions per second and far above any speed a stepper reaches; #Vlimit does not change it, so it does not catch a motor that runs away. Watch the speed in your host and send Send_Idle or Send_ESTOP when it is wrong. Errors and recovery KI-11 Only motion frames and answered status requests reset the watchdog. Setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear, Save) and UART commands do not, so a host that only configures the driver, or a terminal session with a saved watchdog, ends in a watchdog error. While the watchdog runs, send a status request such as Send_Respond_Encoder_data within every watchdog period. Before you work over UART alone, set the watchdog to 0 over CAN and save. Over CAN: a control loop KI-12 The driver error flag (Driver_error, Driver error in #Error) is never raised. STEPFOC reads no fault output of its driver stage, so a stage that shuts down for heat or a short only makes the motor lose torque, with no error. Watch the current and the position in your host; a commanded motor that goes limp points to the driver stage. Lower the current limit and give the board air. Troubleshooting: the driver gets hot KI-13 #Dir stores a flag that #Info prints as Phase direction, but the control code does not use it: it does not reverse the motor. To make the other direction positive, negate the setpoints and the values you read back in your host. Wiring: phase order and direction KI-14 #Mode prints Gripper mode in voltage-torque mode (#Uq), and nothing at all in gripper mode, HALL mode, the angle-offset search and open-loop steps (#gosteps). In those modes go by the command you sent last, not by #Mode. UART commands: status and utility KI-15 In idle the driver brakes, with the coils shorted, at every power-up and also with an error; #Coast is not kept by #Save. The current a turned motor drives through the shorted coils is not limited. Send #Coast (or Send_Settings) after every power-up if the motor must turn freely in idle, and do not let a load drive a braking motor fast. Braking in idle

docs.title: V108 (2026-08-26)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V108 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed calibration (#Cal) spuriously failing with Phase order is wrong! on otherwise-healthy motors. The "confirm commutation" pre-check (before the real angle-offset search) commands a pure torque-axis voltage using the not-yet-calibrated encoder angle — depending on a given unit's actual rotor-to-encoder mounting angle, that command could land almost entirely on the wrong axis and produce ~zero torque, failing the check even though nothing was actually broken. Bench-confirmed on a real unit.
  • Fix: retry the pre-check once at a 90° angle bias before declaring failure — guaranteed to land within 45° of the true torque axis on at least one of the two tries. The downstream angle-offset search is unaffected and already independent of this pre-check.
  • Added Spin-confirm delta / Vbus diagnostics to #Cal's failure report, for the rare case both tries still fail.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
• The controller now drains up to 8 CAN messages per pass instead of just 1, so short bursts (multiple commands sent back-to-back, or a busy multi-node bus) no longer silently drop messages once the 3-deep hardware FIFO fills.
  • A CAN peripheral that fails to initialize no longer bricks the board — UART stays fully usable, only the CAN bus is skipped.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Added a hardware watchdog (100ms). If the control loop ever stops running, the board resets instead of leaving the motor driven at a stale duty cycle.
  • Fixed a bug where Torque_mode could silently overwrite your commanded Iq setpoint when clamping to the current limit — reading it back after clamping now shows what you actually asked for, and raising the current limit afterward immediately restores the original commanded torque instead of requiring the command to be resent.
  • Fixed undefined behavior in a serial-protocol integer conversion (fourBytesToInt).
  • Synced default configuration values that had drifted between two locations in the code, so a fresh #Default and a freshly-flashed board's built-in defaults now agree.

docs.title: EEPROM / configuration integrity
docs.text:
• Added CRC validation over the saved configuration, split into two independent halves: calibration data (resistance, inductance, Kt/KV, angle offset, current-loop gains, etc.) and settings (PID tuning, limits, watchdog config, CAN ID, etc.).
  • This means a corrupted save (e.g. from a power loss mid-write) is detected and safely defaulted instead of silently running with garbage values — and critically, a future firmware update that only adds a new setting can no longer wipe your calibration, since the two are validated independently.
  • Boards upgrading from older, pre-CRC firmware keep their existing calibration automatically — no need to recalibrate after this update.
  • A few unused slots were reserved in the calibration block for upcoming features (e.g. magnet alignment), so those can be added later without another migration.

docs.title: Theory corner
docs.text: The control concepts behind the driver's modes, for readers who want to know why a setting does what it does. Nothing here is needed to use the driver; the chapters say what to type.

docs.title: Field-oriented control of a stepper
docs.text:
A hybrid stepper is a two-phase synchronous motor with many pole pairs: 50 for a 1.8° motor, so one mechanical revolution is 50 electrical cycles. A conventional stepper driver drives it blindly: it advances the current pattern one step at a time and relies on the rotor following. The torque the rotor receives depends on the angle between the stator field and the rotor, the load angle; it is largest a quarter of an electrical cycle ahead of the rotor and zero when the two are aligned. Because the driver does not know where the rotor is, it keeps full current in the coils at all times, so that even a badly placed field produces enough torque, and it still loses steps when the load angle exceeds 90° electrical.

Field-oriented control (FOC) closes that gap with a measurement of the rotor angle. The encoder on the motor shaft gives the mechanical angle \(\theta\); with the pole pairs \(p\) and the angle offset \(\theta_0\) found by calibration, the electrical angle is \(\theta_e = p\,\theta + \theta_0\). The two coil currents \(I_A\) and \(I_B\) are transformed into the rotor's frame of reference (the Park transform):

\[ I_d = I_A \cos\theta_e + I_B \sin\theta_e,\qquad I_q = -I_A \sin\theta_e + I_B \cos\theta_e \]

\(I_q\), the quadrature current, is the part of the current that stands at right angles to the rotor field and produces torque: \(\tau = K_t\, I_q\). \(I_d\), the direct current, is aligned with the field and produces none. Two PI controllers regulate \(I_q\) to the torque demand and \(I_d\) to zero by choosing the voltages \(U_q\) and \(U_d\); the inverse transform turns those into the two coil voltages, applied by PWM at 25 kHz. The loop runs at 6250 Hz.

The consequences are what makes a FOC stepper behave like a servo: the current is only what the torque needs, so the motor runs cool and quiet; the field is always placed where it produces the most torque per ampere; and a step is never lost, because the controller knows the rotor position at every instant and works from the error, not from a count of pulses.

Calibration supplies the constants this needs. The pole pairs come from the step angle. The current loop gains follow from the coil's resistance \(R\) and inductance \(L\) and the chosen bandwidth \(\omega_c = 2\pi f_c\) (#Cbw): \(K_p = L\,\omega_c\) and \(K_i = R\,\omega_c\) cancel the coil's electrical time constant and give a first-order response at \(f_c\). The firmware computes a discrete-time form of these and divides \(K_p\) by an empirical factor of 7, so its gains are softer than the formula. The angle offset is found by locking the rotor with the stator field and reading where it settles, then refined by a sweep for the offset at which the motor turns alike in both directions. In theory the torque constant follows from the velocity constant: in SI units \(K_t = 1/K_V\) (with \(K_V\) in rpm/V, \(K_t \approx 9.55/K_V\) Nm/A). The firmware estimates \(K_V\) from the speed the motor reaches at 500 mA per volt of supply and uses \(K_t = 8.27/K_V\); treat both as estimates.

docs.title: The cascade of loops
docs.text:
Position, velocity and current are controlled by three loops nested inside one another:

\[ \text{position loop: } \omega_d = K_{pp}\,(\theta_d - \theta) \qquad \text{velocity loop: } I_{q,d} = K_{pv}\,(\omega_d - \omega) + K_{iv}\!\int(\omega_d - \omega)\,dt \qquad \text{current loop: } U_q = \text{PI}(I_{q,d} - I_q) \]

The position loop is proportional: its output is a speed demand, limited by the velocity limit. The velocity loop is a PI controller: its output is a current demand, limited by the current limit; the integral term removes the steady-state error a load would otherwise leave. The current loop is the innermost and fastest. Each loop must be slower than the one inside it, by a factor of five to ten, for the inner loop to look like an ideal actuator to the outer one; that is why the loops are tuned from the inside out, and why a current loop bandwidth of 500 Hz leaves room for a velocity loop of a few tens of hertz and a position loop below that.

A command picks where the cascade is entered: a current setpoint uses the current loop alone, a speed setpoint the two inner loops, a position setpoint all three. The feedforward terms the CAN motion frames carry are added to the demands rather than computed from an error: a speed feedforward is added to the position loop's output, a current feedforward to the velocity loop's output. A host that knows the trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct what is left, which gives a faster, smoother response than letting the loops produce the whole demand from the error.

An integrator accumulates error over time, and keeps accumulating while the output is at its limit; the overshoot this causes when the limit is released is windup. The velocity loop's integrator is clamped to the current limit, and #Rstint resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which suits a host that sends one setpoint after another in large steps.

docs.title: Impedance control
docs.text:
Impedance control does not prescribe a motion or a force. It prescribes the relation between the two: how much force the motor produces when it is displaced from its setpoint and how fast. The driver's PD mode implements a spring and a damper around the setpoint:

\[ \tau = K_P\,(\theta_d - \theta) + K_D\,(\dot\theta_d - \dot\theta) + K_t\, I_{ff} \]

with the stiffness \(K_P\) in Nm/rad, the damping \(K_D\) in Nm·s/rad, and a current feedforward \(I_{ff}\) for a known load such as gravity. The torque is produced by the current loop (\(I_q = \tau / K_t\)), which is what makes FOC a prerequisite: a stepper driven blindly cannot produce a commanded torque.

Pushed off its setpoint by an external force \(F\), the motor yields by \(\Delta\theta = \tau_{ext}/K_P\) and pushes back with that force; let go, it returns, with the damper settling the motion. A small \(K_P\) makes a soft joint, a large one a stiff joint; \(K_D\) without \(K_P\) is a pure damper. The setpoint can move, in which case the virtual spring drags the rotor along a trajectory with a bounded force — the property legged robots, hand-guided arms and anything that touches people or an uncertain environment need. The impedance loop is also what a position loop is not: the position loop's integral action removes any steady-state deflection and so makes the joint as stiff as the current limit allows, which is the right thing for a machine tool and the wrong thing for a leg.

The full impedance model includes an inertia term, \(M\ddot\theta\); the driver, like most joint controllers, leaves it out, so the apparent inertia is the motor's own.

docs.title: Admittance control
docs.text:
Admittance is the inverse relation: the controller measures the force and commands a motion,

\[ \dot\theta_d = \frac{\tau_{ext} - K\,(\theta - \theta_0)}{B} \]

on top of a stiff position controller. It is the natural form for a machine that has a force sensor and a position loop that cannot be made soft, such as an industrial arm; impedance control is the natural form for a machine whose actuator is a torque source, such as a FOC motor. The driver has no force sensor and implements impedance; a host that wants admittance behaviour can estimate the external torque from \(K_t I_q\) minus the known load and command positions accordingly, with the limits of that estimate (friction, cogging, the current loop's accuracy).

docs.title: Compliance and stiffness
docs.text:
Stiffness \(K\) is the force per unit of displacement; compliance is its inverse, \(C = 1/K\), the displacement per unit of force. Passive compliance is in the mechanism — a spring, a flexible finger, a belt; active compliance is in the controller — the impedance loop above. The driver offers three points on that scale: the position mode, stiff up to the current limit; the PD mode, as stiff as \(K_P\); and the current mode, which is no stiffness at all, a torque source the host shapes as it likes.

The current limit #Ilim is a force limit in every mode: the largest torque the motor will produce before it yields, whatever the loops ask. Set it for the motor's rating, and for the mechanism's.

docs.title: Which mode
docs.text: Mode Behaviour under an external force Use Position holds the position up to the current limit, then yields positioning, machines, anything that must not deflect Velocity holds the speed up to the current limit conveyors, wheels, spindles PD (impedance) deflects in proportion to the force, returns when released legs, arms that touch things or people, hand guiding, teleoperation Current (torque) produces the commanded torque, moves as the load dictates a host that closes its own loop, gravity compensation, force-limited pressing

docs.title: What is bilateral teleoperation?
docs.text:
Bilateral teleoperation is a concept that Involves two-way communication where both the operator and the remote device send and receive feedback. The operator controls the device remotely and receives sensory feedback (such as force) from the device to adjust their actions.

The two grippers are virtually coupled to each other, allowing either to act as the master (the haptic interface) or the slave (the manipulator) in the system. We are not using a force sensor at the grippers but are relying on proprioception.

Figure 1: Bilateral teleoperation of two coupled grippers.

Watch these example videos to get a "feel" of the concept:

  • 2DOF arm bilateral

What is this used for?

These kind of setup is perfect for: Teleoperation, Imitation learning, Virtual Environments...

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
The magic of this setup is done with these 2 simple formulas.

We got them from amazing Ben Katz paper, creator of mini cheetah quad: Link to the paper

𝜏1,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃2,𝑖 − 𝜃1, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃2,𝑖 − ˙𝜃1,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃1,𝑖)

𝜏2,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃1,𝑖 − 𝜃2, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃1,𝑖 − ˙𝜃2,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃2,𝑖)

docs.title: What is Gravity Compensation?
docs.text: Gravity compensation is a fundamental concept in robotic control that helps counteract the effects of gravity on a robot's joints and links. By applying the necessary motor current to balance this torque, the robotic joint can remain stationary at any position without additional external forces.

docs.title: Why is it so important?
docs.text: In robotics, a significant portion of motor power is consumed just fighting against gravity. Gravity compensation algorithms are standard in all industrial robots and collaborative robot arms because they provide: improved position accuracy and control, smoother motion planning, and more precise force control applications. The gravity compensation algorithm works as a feedforward component to the motor PID control loops, reducing their computational load and improving overall performance.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
In this example, we use the Robotics Toolbox for Python to model a "robotic arm" with a single revolute joint. We compute the required torque using the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) and convert this torque into a motor current/torque that the motor controller will command the motor.

The full write-up is the blog post Gravity compensation in robotics. The example code is in Gravity compensation in the Python library's examples, with its bill of materials.

docs.title: Follow a specific trajectory
docs.text:
Joint level control involves directly controlling the angles or positions of the robot's individual joints. Each joint is treated as an independent actuator, and the control system sends commands to each joint to achieve the desired angles.

For this example we will not use joint level control but a different method called Task/Cartesian Level Control. Task or cartesian level control focuses on controlling the position and orientation of the robot's end-effector in a Cartesian coordinate system (X, Y, Z coordinates and orientations). In our robot leg case we don't have Z axes (or orientation) and our end-effector is foot (end of our robot leg).

In this example we will follow a circle trajectory i X,Y plane. We defined that trajectory with our function generate_circle_coords and with parameters:

  • center - Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters
  • radius - Radius of the circle in meters
  • speed - Speed of the end-effector in meters per second
  • time_var - Elapsed time in seconds
Figure 5: The circle the foot traced at speed 1 and at speed 3.

How precise you follow the trajectory depends on the speed you set. With low speeds you can track the circle perfectly. With larger speeds the system can't keep up and overshoots. This is due multiple reaseons like:

  • Inertia and Momentum: At higher speeds, the inertia and momentum of the robot leg increase, making it harder to change directions quickly and accurately.
  • Centrifugal and Coriolis Forces
  • Trajectory Planning and Execution - at higher speeds our trajectory has less points to create a full circle. This is due a fixed rate we send data to our motors eg. every 20ms.
  • Feedforward Control: Lack of proper feedforward control can lead to errors in trajectory tracking, as the controller might not anticipate the required accelerations and decelerations.

You can see that from the example with speed set to 1 and 3.

import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox

import numpy as np
# We are using v1.1.0
from roboticstoolbox import DHRobot, RevoluteDH, ERobot, ELink, ETS
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *

import math
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([14000,2430]) # These are the positions we got from calib code
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 0.90476190] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

Motor_values = np.array([0,0])

# robot length values (metres)

# Create robot model using DH params
L1 = RevoluteDH(a=l[0],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[0])
L2 = RevoluteDH(a=l[1],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[1])
robot = DHRobot([L1,L2], name="Two link")

prev_pos = np.array([0,0])
speed_var = np.array([0,0])

def generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time):
  """
  Generates x,y coordinates for a circle at a given time, considering constant speed.

  Args:
      center: Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters.
      radius: Radius of the circle in meters.
      speed: Speed of the end-effector in meters per second.
      time: Elapsed time in seconds.

  Returns:
      Tuple containing the x and y coordinates in meters.
  """

  # Calculate angular displacement based on speed and time
  angular_displacement = speed * time

  # Use parametric equations for a circle to generate coordinates
  x = center[0] + radius * math.cos(angular_displacement)
  y = center[1] + radius * math.sin(angular_displacement)

Script that will plot the data of your leg:

plot_leg_data.py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_data(filename):
  """
  Plots data from a text file in the format:
  x1, y1
  x2, y2
  ...

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file containing the data.
  """

  try:
    with open(filename, 'r') as file:
      data = file.readlines()

    x_data = []
    y_data = []
    for line in data:
      # Split the line based on comma (",")
      values = line.strip().split(',')

      # Check if there are exactly two values per line
      if len(values) != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid line format in file '{filename}': {line}")

      try:
        x = float(values[0])
        y = float(values[1])
      except ValueError:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid data type in file '{filename}': {line}")

      x_data.append(x)
      y_data.append(y)

    # Ensure equal x and y scales
    plt.axis('equal')

    # Create the plot
    plt.plot(x_data, y_data)

    # Customize the plot (optional)
    plt.xlabel('X-Position')
    plt.ylabel('Y-Position')
    plt.title('Data Plot from ' + filename)

    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

  except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: File '{filename}' not found.")
  except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

docs.title: Where the facts come from
docs.text: The command IDs, the frame lengths the firmware accepts, the responses it sends, the list of UART commands with their kind (Set/Get, Get or action), their argument type, the mode each enters and what it prints, and the defaults are read from the firmware's source at its release tag by tools/sync_firmware.py in the documentation repository, and the pages are built from that at every build. The descriptions, units and byte layouts are written by hand, and the build fails when they name a command the firmware does not have, or miss one it has, or when a byte layout does not fit the frame. The firmware version is in the version box on the landing page.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Bytes are numbered from 0, the first byte on the bus (data[0]). Multi-byte values are big-endian: the most significant byte first. Floats are IEEE 754 single precision in 4 bytes.
  • Bits inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit: bit 7 is the first flag the firmware packs into the byte, bit 0 the last.
  • Encoder ticks: 16384 per revolution; speeds in ticks per second; currents in mA; voltages in mV.
  • UART command names are case-sensitive and spelled exactly as the firmware compares them.

docs.title: CAN frame tool and downloads
docs.text: Build or inspect a frame using the command definitions of this manual's firmware release. All calculations run in your browser; the tool does not connect to an adapter or send commands to hardware.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Command definitions (JSON) · Position DBC · Velocity DBC · Current DBC

The JSON includes the firmware tag, source commit, message IDs, every documented layout and its bit order. The DBC files cover nodes 0 to 13, with both the clean and fault-bit identifiers of driver replies. Reserved commands are omitted. Values use the firmware's native units: ticks, ticks/s, mA and the units in the CAN reference.

Choose the DBC for the Send_data_pack_1 layout your host sends:

File Command layout Position DBC 8 bytes: position, speed feedforward, current feedforward Velocity DBC 5 bytes: speed, current feedforward Current DBC 2 bytes: current

The three layouts share a CAN identifier. DBC cannot select a layout from the frame's length, so load the matching file; the browser decoder below handles all three lengths. Other message layouts are the same in each download.

An RTR request uses the same identifier as its data reply. DBC describes the data reply; it does not represent the request's RTR flag or the empty gripper status poll. Both are supported by the browser tool.

The gripper's two object-detection bits have an unusual order: bit 5 is the low bit, bit 4 the high bit. The DBC signal gripper_object_detection_raw retains the wire value and supplies text labels (raw 2 = object while closing, raw 1 = object while opening). The browser decoder converts that pair to the firmware's numeric status (1 = closing, 2 = opening).

docs.title: Clearing
docs.text: #Clear and Send_Clear_Error clear every flag except Calibrated and go to idle; a flag whose cause persists is set again at once. The watchdog, E-stop and velocity errors clear and stay clear; the Vbus, encoder and temperature errors come back until the cause is gone, and so does a gripper E-stop while its E-stop bit is 1. Calibration clears the calibration error.

Object detection in the library

Library version 1.20 assembles gripper_object_detection with the two bits swapped relative to the firmware, so it reports 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object detected while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object detected while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. docs.title: CAN protocol
docs.text:
CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. The identifier carries the node ID (bits 10 to 7, 0 to 15), the command ID (bits 6 to 1, 0 to 63) and, in frames from the driver, the error bit (bit 0). Over CAN explains how the pieces are used; this page lists them.

Three kinds of message:

  • Send_… — the host sends data to the driver. A few are answered (the motion commands with Respond_data_pack_1, the gripper command with Respond_Gripper_data_pack); most are not.
  • Send_Respond_… — the host asks for data with a remote frame (RTR bit set, no data) under the command ID; the driver answers with a data frame under the same command ID.
  • Respond_… — frames only the driver sends.

Multi-byte values are big-endian (data[0] first); floats are IEEE 754 single precision; bits inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit (bit 7 first).

docs.title: Send_data_pack_1
docs.text:
ID 2host → driver2 or 5 or 8 bytesPython: Send_data_pack_1()

The motion command. Its length decides the control mode the driver enters: 8 bytes command a position with a speed and a current feedforward, 5 bytes a speed with a current feedforward, 2 bytes a current. Send 0 for a feedforward you do not use. A frame of any other length is ignored (the driver flags it as a wrong data length) but still answered.

8 bytes — position setpoint with speed and current feedforward (position mode)

Byte Bit Field Type Meaning 0-2 Position setpoint signed 24-bit encoder ticks 3-5 Speed feedforward signed 24-bit encoder ticks/s 6-7 Current feedforward signed 16-bit mA

5 bytes — speed setpoint with current feedforward (velocity mode)

Byte Bit Field Type Meaning 0-2 Speed setpoint signed 24-bit encoder ticks/s 3-4 Current feedforward signed 16-bit mA

2 bytes — current setpoint (current mode)

Byte Bit Field Type Meaning 0-1 Current setpoint signed 16-bit mA

The driver answers with Respond_data_pack_1.

Every form resets the watchdog. With Rstint set, the integral accumulators are cleared on each new setpoint.

ID 4host → driver8 bytesPython: Send_data_pack_PD()

Puts the driver in impedance (PD) mode and sets the position, speed and current feedforward of the PD loop, whose gains are KP and KD (Send_PD_Gains).

8 bytes

The driver answers with Respond_data_pack_1.

Firmware 106 and older wrote the speed into the feedforward instead of the PD loop's speed setpoint, so the speed term had no effect; 107 fixed it.

docs.title: Send_data_pack_HALL
docs.text:
ID 31host → driver4 bytesPython: Send_data_pack_HALL()

Homing against a sensor: the driver spins at the given speed until the input on the ADDITIONAL2 pin shows the trigger condition, then latches the position it reached as its position setpoint and holds it. With a level trigger (0 or 1) it holds only while the pin stays at that level: when the pin changes back, the driver spins on again until the level returns. The edge trigger (2) holds after the first edge. Sending the command again while the driver is already in HALL mode does not re-arm it; leave the mode first.

4 bytes

Byte Bit Field Type Meaning 0-2 Speed signed 24-bit encoder ticks/s; the sign gives the direction 3 Trigger unsigned 8-bit 0 = trigger when the pin is low, 1 = when it is high, 2 = on any edge

The driver answers with Respond_data_hall.

Firmware 103 read only bit 7 of byte 3 (0 or 1); the edge trigger (2) came later.
